seoTitle: How to Delete TradingView Chart Layouts (2026)
metaDescription: Clear out old TradingView chart layouts — find the layout menu in the chart toolbar, open the Layouts manager, and delete the setups you no longer use.
intro: Anyone who tests more than one strategy on TradingView ends up with a graveyard of saved layouts: half-finished setups, one-off experiments, and copies of copies with names that meant something six months ago. They clutter the layout switcher, slow down the moment you actually need to find the right chart, and on a free account they count against the small number of saved layouts you're allowed. Deleting them takes seconds once you know that the control lives in the chart's top toolbar rather than in account settings. This guide shows the two places layouts appear, how to delete from the manager, and what to check before you remove something you can't get back.

steps.heading: Find the layout name in the chart toolbar
steps.body: Open any chart on TradingView and look along the top toolbar, to the right of the timeframe buttons and drawing tools. The name of the layout you currently have loaded sits there next to a small cloud icon — in a working account it might read something like "Idle For Testing" rather than anything descriptive. That name is also a button. Everything to do with saving, renaming, copying, and deleting layouts hangs off it, which is why searching your profile or account settings for a layout manager turns up nothing.

image.caption: A TradingView chart with the active layout name shown in the top toolbar, just left of the Publish button.

steps.heading: Open the layout menu
steps.body: Clicking the layout name drops down the layout menu. At the top are actions for the layout you're currently in — Save layout, an Autosave toggle, Sharing, Make a copy, Rename, and Export chart data — followed by Create new layout. Below that, under Recently used, TradingView lists the handful of layouts you've opened most recently with their symbol and timeframe underneath each name. This recent list is a shortcut, not your full collection, so don't be alarmed if a layout you're hunting for isn't visible here.

image.caption: The layout dropdown open over the chart, with save and rename actions at the top and a Recently used list below.

steps.heading: Open the full Layouts manager
steps.body: At the bottom of that dropdown is Open layout, which has the keyboard shortcut Dot next to it. Choosing it opens the Layouts dialog — the complete list of every chart layout attached to your account, with a search box at the top and a sort control on the right. Each row shows the layout name plus the symbol, timeframe, and the date it was last saved, which is usually the fastest way to identify dead weight: a layout last touched two years ago on a symbol you no longer trade is a safe candidate for deletion.

image.caption: The Layouts dialog listing every saved layout with its symbol, timeframe, and last-saved date, and a delete icon on the highlighted row.

steps.heading: Delete the layouts you don't need
steps.body: Hover over a row in the Layouts list and a trash icon appears at the right-hand end of it, along with a star for marking favourites. Click the trash icon and confirm to remove that layout. TradingView deletes layouts one at a time rather than offering a multi-select, so a proper clear-out is a short session of repeated clicks. Deletion is permanent — a removed layout doesn't go to any kind of recycle bin, and the drawings, indicator settings, and templates saved inside it go with it. If a layout contains work you might want later, use Make a copy or Export chart data before you delete, or rename it to something like "archive-" and leave it.

steps.heading: Watch the layout limit on free accounts
steps.body: Layout housekeeping matters more on the free plan, which allows only a single saved chart layout, while paid tiers step up from a handful to unlimited depending on the plan. If TradingView refuses to save a new layout, you have hit that ceiling rather than encountered a bug, and clearing out an old layout is the fix. It's worth knowing this before you start a new strategy: deleting to make room mid-session is exactly the situation where people delete the wrong thing in a hurry.

steps.heading: Rename what's left so it stays clean
steps.body: The clear-out only holds if the survivors have names you'll recognize in three months. Rename from the same layout dropdown and use a convention that carries the information the list already shows you well — asset class and purpose beat version numbers, so "Crypto swing" and "NIFTY intraday" work better than "Chart 3" and "test2". Star the two or three layouts you genuinely use daily so they sort to the top of the manager. A short naming pass now saves you from repeating this whole cleanup next quarter.

faq.question: Where is the delete option for a TradingView layout?
faq.answer: Click the layout name in the chart's top toolbar, choose Open layout at the bottom of the dropdown, then hover the layout you want to remove in the Layouts dialog and click the trash icon on its row.

faq.question: Can I recover a chart layout after deleting it?
faq.answer: No. Deletion is permanent and takes the drawings and indicator settings saved in that layout with it. Use Make a copy or Export chart data first if there's anything you might want back.

faq.question: How many layouts can I save on a free TradingView account?
faq.answer: The free plan allows one saved chart layout; paid plans raise the limit progressively up to unlimited. If a save is refused, you have reached your plan's limit rather than hit a fault.

faq.question: Can I delete several layouts at once?
faq.answer: Not in the Layouts manager — there is no multi-select. You delete them one row at a time, which is quick but tedious if you have a long backlog.

faq.question: Can I delete layouts from the TradingView mobile app?
faq.answer: Yes. Layouts live on your account rather than on a device, so opening the layout list in the mobile app shows the same collection, and removing one there removes it everywhere.
